sessions.title: A direction the map does not turn away
sessions.focus: Define eigenvectors/eigenvalues from invariant one-dimensional directions, distinguish direction preservation from fixed vectors or preserved length, and derive repeated action along one eigenvector.
sessions.purpose: M14 taught what a linear map does to arbitrary vectors. M16 begins by asking whether any nonzero directions are special enough that the map only rescales them; the concept must exist before the characteristic-polynomial recipe.
sessions.centralCapability: Given a finite real linear map and fresh candidate vectors, verify or refute eigenvector status from Av=λv, interpret the invariant line, and use λ to predict repeated action along that direction.
sessions.principalObstacle: A learner may confuse Av=v with Av=λv, preserved norm with preserved direction, or allow v=0 because A0=λ0 for every λ.
entryPrerequisites: M13 nonzero vectors, scalar multiples and span(v)
M14 matrix-vector action and finite linear maps
M02/M09 scalar powers for repeated action
requiredOwnership: Verify eigenpair status Av=λv for supplied nonzero real candidates by exact proportionality, recovering λ when it exists.
Use linearity to justify that a nonzero scalar rescaling of a verified eigenvector represents the same eigendirection and retains the same eigenvalue.
Distinguish preserved direction from fixed-vector or preserved-length claims and use a verified eigenpair to justify a specified repeated action A^k v=λ^k v.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real 2D/3D linear maps; candidate directions are checked directly without characteristic polynomials.
sessions.transferScope: Audit an orthogonal rotation that preserves length but has no nonzero real eigenvector, forcing the learner to reject preserved-length reasoning.
inScope: repeated action on a verified eigenvector
sessions.exitCondition: On a fresh linear map, verify/refute candidate eigenvectors, identify λ when it exists, explain the invariant line and use the verified eigenpair to predict repeated action without matrix-power brute force.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. M14 taught us to apply a linear map to any vector. Now ask a more structural question: is there a nonzero direction that the map does not turn away from itself? If A sends a nonzero vector v to a scalar multiple of itself, Av=λv, then v is an eigenvector and λ is its eigenvalue. The line span(v) is invariant because every point cv on that line is sent to A(cv)=cAv=cλv, which is still on the same line.

Definition discipline. The vector must be nonzero. If v=0 were admitted, A0=λ0 would hold for every λ and the word eigenvalue would stop identifying anything. The scalar λ is allowed to be zero: for P=diag(1,0), e2=(0,1) is nonzero and Pe2=0=0e2. A negative λ reverses orientation along the same line; |λ|>1 stretches and |λ|<1 shrinks. Only λ=1 makes every eigenvector on that line a fixed vector.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[0,1]]. For e1=(1,0), Ae1=(2,0)=2e1, so e1 is an eigenvector with λ=2. For w=(1,-1), Aw=(1,-1)=w, so w is an eigenvector with λ=1. But e2=(0,1) maps to (1,1), which is not a scalar multiple of e2, so e2 is not an eigenvector. The decisive test is exact proportionality, not whether the image merely looks similar.

Connect. If Av=λv and c≠0, then A(cv)=cAv=cλv=λ(cv), so all nonzero vectors on the same invariant line share the same eigenvalue. This is about a direction/subspace, even though we represent it by particular nonzero vectors.

Repeated action. Once Av=λv, apply A again: A²v=A(λv)=λAv=λ²v. Induction gives A^k v=λ^k v for every integer k≥0. This conclusion is earned only after the eigenpair is verified.

Guided practice. Let C=[[3,0],[2,1]]. Test u=(1,1), v=(0,1), and r=(1,0). For every eigenvector, identify λ and the invariant line. Then predict C^4u without multiplying four matrices.

Fade. The fixed Main changes both the matrix and candidate directions; the Transfer changes the representation entirely to a rotation audit. No fixed answer is solved in the lesson.

Distinction check. Fixed vector means λ=1. Preserved length says ||Av||=||v||. Eigenvector says Av is exactly a real scalar multiple of the nonzero v. These are different properties.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. Cu=(3,3)=3u, so u has λ=3 and invariant line span(1,1). Cv=(0,1)=v, so v has λ=1 and invariant line span(0,1). Cr=(3,2) is not proportional to r, so r is not an eigenvector. Therefore C^4u=3^4u=81(1,1)=(81,81).

sessions.title: An eigenspace is a kernel
sessions.focus: Rewrite Av=λv as (A-λI)v=0, identify E_λ as a null space, and separate the eigenspace subspace from its nonzero eigenvectors.
sessions.purpose: S01 identified special directions one candidate at a time. S02 turns one verified eigenvalue into the full family of vectors sharing it, using M14 null-space structure before any characteristic-polynomial machinery appears.
sessions.centralCapability: For a supplied real λ, form A-λI, solve its homogeneous system, report a basis/span for E_λ, and distinguish the zero vector's membership in the eigenspace from the nonzero requirement for eigenvectors.
sessions.principalObstacle: The equation Av=λv is treated as a one-vector check rather than a homogeneous system; alternatively the zero vector is either wrongly excluded from E_λ or wrongly promoted to an eigenvector.
entryPrerequisites: S01 eigenpair definition and invariant line
M14 homogeneous systems and null spaces
requiredOwnership: For a supplied real λ, rewrite Av=λv as (A-λI)v=0 and compute E_λ=Null(A-λI) as a span/basis.
Distinguish the eigenspace E_λ, which is a subspace containing 0, from the set of eigenvectors for λ, which consists of the nonzero vectors in E_λ.
Audit whether a proposed set of eigenvectors is itself an eigenspace by checking subspace requirements and the zero-vector boundary.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact finite real square matrices with λ supplied; systematic discovery of λ remains S03.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that removes zero from a correct eigenline and then incorrectly calls the resulting set an eigenspace.
sessions.exitCondition: Given A and a supplied λ, compute the entire eigenspace and state exactly which members are eigenvectors.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S01 let us test one candidate v. But once λ is known, we want every vector with that eigenvalue. Start from Av=λv and move all terms to one side: (A-λI)v=0. M14 already taught how to solve a homogeneous system, so the new object is built from an old one.

Define. For a fixed scalar λ, the eigenspace is E_λ={v:Av=λv}=Null(A-λI). Because every null space is a subspace, E_λ contains 0 and is closed under linear combinations. Eigenvectors for λ are the nonzero members of E_λ. So “eigenspace” and “set of eigenvectors” are not literally the same set.

Worked example. Let A=[[2,1],[0,2]] and suppose λ=2 is supplied. Then A-2I=[[0,1],[0,0]]. Solving (A-2I)(x,y)^T=0 gives y=0 and x free, so E_2=span{(1,0)}. Every nonzero (t,0) is an eigenvector with λ=2; (0,0) belongs to E_2 but is not an eigenvector. If instead λ=1 is supplied, A-I=[[1,1],[0,1]] has only the zero solution, so E_1={0}; therefore 1 is not an eigenvalue.

Connect. This uses no new elimination theorem. The only new move is recognizing the eigenvector equation as a null-space problem for the shifted matrix A-λI.

Guided practice. Let B=[[3,0,0],[0,3,1],[0,0,1]] and take λ=3. Form B-3I, solve the homogeneous system, give a basis for E_3, and state which vectors in that eigenspace are eigenvectors.

Fade. Main supplies a new 3x3 matrix and two λ values. Transfer stops being a calculation and instead asks whether a proposed punctured line is an eigenspace.

Distinction check. E_λ must include zero because it is a null space. The zero vector is nevertheless never called an eigenvector. If Null(A-λI)={0}, then there is no eigenvector for that λ.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. B-3I=[[0,0,0],[0,0,1],[0,0,-2]], so z=0 while x,y are free. Thus E_3=span{(1,0,0),(0,1,0)}. Every nonzero vector in this plane is an eigenvector with λ=3; the zero vector is in E_3 but is not an eigenvector.

sessions.title: Why the characteristic equation appears
sessions.focus: Derive det(A-λI)=0 from the need for a nonzero null-space solution, solve exact low-degree characteristic equations, and return to eigenspaces rather than stopping at roots.
sessions.purpose: S02 can recover E_λ once λ is supplied. S03 earns a systematic way to discover candidate λ values from M14 singularity/determinant structure without turning the determinant equation into the definition of eigenvalue.
sessions.centralCapability: Derive the characteristic equation from Av=λv and singularity, solve it for a small exact matrix, and compute the corresponding eigenspaces.
sessions.principalObstacle: The learner may memorize det(A-λI)=0 as a magic recipe, confuse det(A) with an eigenvalue, or stop after roots without verifying nonzero eigenspaces.
requiredOwnership: Derive det(A-λI)=0 from the requirement that (A-λI)v=0 have a nonzero solution.
Compute the characteristic polynomial/equation for an exact 2×2 or manageable triangular 3×3 matrix and solve for its real eigenvalues.
For each computed eigenvalue, return to Null(A-λI) to construct an eigenspace rather than treating a polynomial root alone as the full eigenpair result.
sessions.applicationScope: Exact small real square matrices whose characteristic polynomial is readily factorable or otherwise solvable with earlier algebra.
sessions.transferScope: Audit a report that mistakes det(A) itself for an eigenvalue and repair the complete eigenvalue/eigenspace analysis.
sessions.exitCondition: From a fresh small matrix, justify the determinant equation, solve the eigenvalues and recover every corresponding eigenspace.
sessions.lesson:
Orient. S02 answered: if λ is known, solve Null(A-λI). Now reverse the question. Which λ make that null space contain something besides 0?

Connect. M14 says a square matrix B has a nonzero solution to Bv=0 exactly when B is singular, and B is singular exactly when det(B)=0. Apply that theorem to the same object B=A-λI. Therefore Av=λv with v≠0 is possible exactly when det(A-λI)=0. This determinant equation is a consequence of the eigenvector definition plus M14 singularity; it is not the definition.

Define. Using the convention p_A(t)=det(A-tI), p_A is the characteristic polynomial. Its roots are the eigenvalues. Some books use det(tI-A); for an n×n matrix that differs by the factor (-1)^n and has the same roots.

Worked example. Let A=[[3,1],[1,3]]. Then A-tI=[[3-t,1],[1,3-t]], so p_A(t)=(3-t)^2-1=t^2-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4). Thus λ=2,4. For λ=4, A-4I=[[-1,1],[1,-1]], whose null space is span{(1,1)}. For λ=2, A-2I=[[1,1],[1,1]], whose null space is span{(1,-1)}. Direct multiplication verifies both eigenpairs.

Explain the logic chain. Nonzero eigenvector → nontrivial kernel of A-λI → shifted matrix singular → determinant zero. Solving the determinant only produces candidate λ values; the eigenspace calculation tells us the actual directions.

Guided practice. Let B=[[2,2],[1,3]]. Form p_B(t), factor it, find its real eigenvalues, and compute a basis for the eigenspace of the larger eigenvalue. Finish with a direct Bv=λv check.

Fade. Main requires the whole derivation/computation on a new matrix. Transfer supplies a plausible but invalid det(A)=λ shortcut and asks for diagnosis plus repair.

Distinction check. det(A) is one scalar attached to A. The eigenvalue condition uses det(A-λI)=0, an equation in the unknown λ. Never replace one with the other.
sessions.guidedFeedback: Check after attempting. p_B(t)=(2-t)(3-t)-2=t^2-5t+4=(t-1)(t-4), so λ=1,4. For λ=4, B-4I=[[-2,2],[1,-1]], giving x=y and E_4=span{(1,1)}. Indeed B(1,1)=(4,4).

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.prompt: Let A=[[1,2],[2,1]]. Consider p=(1,1), q=(2,-2), and r=(1,0). (a) For each candidate, compute Av and decide whether it is an eigenvector over R; when it is, state λ. (b) Explain why q and (1,-1) represent the same eigendirection and must have the same eigenvalue; include the general linearity step A(cv)=λ(cv) for c≠0 once Av=λv. (c) Without multiplying A by itself five times, compute A^5 p and justify the shortcut from the verified eigenpair.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-T@1.prompt: Let R=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. A report says: “R preserves the length of every vector, so every nonzero vector is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 1; in particular e1=(1,0) is fixed.” Audit the report. Give a decisive geometric or algebraic reason that the length claim does not imply the eigenvector claim, test e1 directly, and determine whether R has any nonzero real eigenvector.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-M@1.prompt: Let A=[[4,1,0],[0,4,0],[0,0,2]]. (a) With λ=4 supplied, form A-4I, solve (A-4I)v=0, and give a basis/span description of E_4. (b) Repeat for the supplied λ=2. (c) For each eigenspace, state whether 0 belongs to it and which members are actually eigenvectors.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-T@1.prompt: Let C=[[5,0],[0,1]]. A report writes E_5={t(1,0): t≠0} and says: “This is the eigenspace for 5 because every vector in the set is an eigenvector; the zero vector should be excluded because it is not an eigenvector.” Audit the report. Give the actual E_5, explain whether the reported set is a subspace, and reconcile the role of 0.

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-M@1.prompt: Let A=[[4,2],[1,3]]. Starting from Av=λv with v≠0: (a) state the shifted homogeneous system and explain why a nonzero solution forces det(A-λI)=0; (b) compute and factor p_A(λ)=det(A-λI), then find all real eigenvalues; (c) compute a basis for each eigenspace and verify one eigenpair directly.

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-T@1.prompt: Let T=[[2,1],[0,3]]. A report says: “det(T)=6, therefore 6 is the eigenvalue.” Audit the inference. Write the correct characteristic equation, find all real eigenvalues, and give a basis for each eigenspace.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.reference: Ap=(3,3)=3p, so p is an eigenvector with λ=3. Aq=(-2,2)=-q, so q is an eigenvector with λ=-1. Ar=(1,2), not a scalar multiple of r, so r is not an eigenvector. Since q=2(1,-1), both nonzero vectors lie on the same invariant line; if Av=λv then A(cv)=λ(cv) for c≠0, so they share λ=-1. Finally A^5p=3^5p=243(1,1)=(243,243).

rubric.criterion: Computes all three images and correctly classifies p, q and r, including λ=3 and λ=-1 for the eigenvectors.
Uses linearity to show that nonzero scalar rescaling preserves the eigendirection and eigenvalue, and applies it correctly to q and (1,-1).
Uses the verified eigenpair Ap=3p to justify A^5p=3^5p=(243,243) without brute-force matrix powers.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-M@1.marking: Score only public obligations. Accept any exact proportionality argument and any valid derivation of the repeated-action result.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-T@1.reference: R is a 90-degree rotation, so it preserves Euclidean length but changes every nonzero real direction. Re1=(0,1)≠e1 and is not a scalar multiple of e1. Algebraically, if R(a,b)=λ(a,b) with real λ and (a,b)≠(0,0), then -b=λa and a=λb. Substitution gives (1+λ^2)a=0; if a=0 then b=0, contradiction, so λ^2=-1, impossible for real λ. Thus R has no nonzero real eigenvector. Preserved norm is not preserved direction.

rubric.criterion: Separates length preservation from eigenvector direction preservation and rejects the report's inference.
Tests e1 directly and shows Re1=(0,1) is not a scalar multiple of e1.
Correctly concludes there is no nonzero real eigenvector, with a decisive geometric rotation argument or equivalent real algebraic derivation.

T22V3::SIDE279::S01-T@1.marking: Do not require complex-number notation. A correct geometric 90-degree-rotation proof or the real equation λ^2=-1 is sufficient.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-M@1.reference: For λ=4, A-4I=[[0,1,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,-2]], so y=0,z=0,x is free and E_4=span{(1,0,0)}. For λ=2, A-2I=[[2,1,0],[0,2,0],[0,0,0]], so y=0,x=0,z is free and E_2=span{(0,0,1)}. The zero vector belongs to both eigenspaces because each is a null space, but the eigenvectors are precisely the nonzero members of the corresponding eigenspace.

rubric.criterion: Correctly forms A-4I, solves the homogeneous system and reports E_4=span{(1,0,0)}.
Correctly forms A-2I, solves the homogeneous system and reports E_2=span{(0,0,1)}.
States that 0 belongs to each eigenspace but is not an eigenvector, so only nonzero members are eigenvectors.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-M@1.marking: Accept equivalent parametrizations/bases. Score the zero-vector distinction only if both membership in the eigenspace and exclusion from eigenvectors are correct.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-T@1.reference: The actual eigenspace is E_5=Null(C-5I)=span{(1,0)}={t(1,0):t∈R}. The reported punctured line contains only eigenvectors, but it is not a subspace because it omits 0 (and thus cannot be a null space). Zero must be included in E_5 even though zero itself is not an eigenvector. Hence the set of eigenvectors for 5 is E_5\{0}, not E_5 itself.

rubric.criterion: Gives E_5=span{(1,0)} with all real scalar multiples, including 0.
Explains that the punctured line is not a subspace because it omits 0.
Correctly distinguishes the eigenspace from its nonzero eigenvectors and reconciles why 0 belongs to one but not the other.

T22V3::SIDE279::S02-T@1.marking: Accept any correct subspace argument; omission of zero is already decisive.

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-M@1.reference: From Av=λv, (A-λI)v=0. Because v≠0, A-λI has a nontrivial null space, hence is singular, so det(A-λI)=0. Here det(A-λI)=(4-λ)(3-λ)-2=λ^2-7λ+10=(λ-5)(λ-2), so λ=5,2. For λ=5, Null(A-5I)=span{(2,1)}. For λ=2, Null(A-2I)=span{(-1,1)} (equivalently span{(1,-1)}). For example A(2,1)=(10,5)=5(2,1).

rubric.criterion: Derives the determinant condition through the nontrivial-kernel/singularity chain rather than presenting it as the eigenvector definition.
Computes p_A(λ)=λ^2-7λ+10=(λ-5)(λ-2) and finds eigenvalues 5 and 2.
Computes correct bases E_5=span{(2,1)} and E_2=span{(-1,1)} or equivalent nonzero rescalings.
Directly verifies at least one resulting eigenpair in Av=λv.

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-M@1.marking: Accept the opposite characteristic-polynomial sign convention if roots and subsequent eigenspaces are correct.

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-T@1.reference: det(T)=6 is a determinant value of T; it is not the eigenvalue condition. The correct equation is det(T-λI)=(2-λ)(3-λ)=0, so λ=2,3. E_2=span{(1,0)}. E_3=span{(1,1)}. Thus the report uses the wrong mathematical object in place of the shifted singularity equation.

rubric.criterion: Rejects det(T)=6⇒λ=6 and identifies the missing shifted determinant det(T-λI).
Computes E_2=span{(1,0)} and E_3=span{(1,1)} (up to nonzero rescaling).

T22V3::SIDE279::S03-T@1.marking: A correct explanation that det(T)=6 is not the characteristic equation is sufficient; no product-of-eigenvalues theorem is required.
